examples.solution_text:
Circle A: the marked line joins the centre to the circumference, so the radius is already given.

$r = 4\text{ m}$

Circle B: the marked line passes through the centre across the whole circle, so halve the diameter.

$\begin{aligned}r &= \frac{d}{2}\\ &= \frac{6}{2}\\ &= 3\text{ m}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A circle has a diameter of $\frac{5}{7}\text{ cm}$. Find its radius in centimetres, as a fraction.
examples.solution_text:
The radius is half the diameter. Dividing a fraction by $2$ doubles its denominator.

$\begin{aligned}r &= \frac{d}{2}\\ &= \frac{5}{7}\div 2\\ &= \frac{5}{14}\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$

coverage.summary: Authored three examples covering all distinct assessed methods. Whole-number, odd-number, decimal and worded diameters share the same halving method. Questions and solutions are separate; solution prose and mathematics inherit renderer blue. Diagrams use black ink and explicit 10 pt labels, with derived annotations confined to the solution. No existing examples were present. Assessment mappings classify methods only; accepted practice and quiz mathematics were neither changed nor re-audited. Independent example review and final rendered verification remain for the coordinator.

examples.derivation: The marked segment spans the circle through its centre, so d = 11 cm. Independently, r = d/2 = 11/2 cm = 5.5 cm. Both solution half-segment labels agree. The supplied radius–diameter review and Key Ideas support this method.

Circle A marks a centre-to-circumference segment, giving r = 4 m directly. Circle B marks a full diameter through the centre, giving r = 6/2 = 3 m. The supplied identification review supports distinguishing these segments and halving only the diameter.
Independently, r = (5/7)/2 = (5/7)(1/2) = 5/14 cm. The supplied radius–diameter table rows h–k support fractional halving. A diagram is unnecessary for this explicitly stated diameter.
